item.content:encoded:
G-7 to launch exercises to guard against AI cyberattacks Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama spoke to reporters during the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Oct 15. PHOTO: BLOOMBERG

Published   Oct 16, 2026, 01:53 PM

Updated   Oct 16, 2026, 01:53 PM

Set as preferred source

BANGKOK – Finance leaders of the Group of Seven (G-7) grouping agreed to hold tabletop exercises to guard against AI cyberattacks, Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said, as policymakers increasingly seek to coordinate responses to growing cyber security risks. The agreement comes after the International Monetary Fund warned this week that confidence could be undermined by an AI-enabled cyberattack on a critical service of a financial institution. “The G7 finance deputies had been discussing the idea of doing tabletop exercises on frontier AI, which was signed off at the ministerial level,” Katayama told reporters on Oct 15.

She made the remarks after attending a meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors of the G-7 advanced economies held on the sidelines of the IMF’s annual gathering in Bangkok, the Thai capital. The plan will feature simulations evolved by G-7 finance authorities to test how they can respond to AI-driven cyberattacks, said a Japanese finance ministry official who attended the finance leaders’ meeting. The results will test effectiveness of existing protocols and be used to revise manuals to better tackle such incidents, the official told reporters.

The exercises by G-7 finance ministries and central banks could include private financial institutions depending on the nature of simulations, the official added. Banking regulators globally are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, Reuters reported, with some pointing to the potential for cyberattacks on banks or rogue agents undermining global financial stability. Among them is the Bank of England, which is working with banks on deep cyber-recovery options, its deputy governor said on Oct 15, adding that they can no longer assume their defences are immune to AI-enabled cyberattacks. REUTERS
